QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Economists have been asked a double-barrelled question -- where do they see 10-year bond yields at the end of 1997, and what do they expect the spread to U.S. 10-year Treasuries to be.

The market will be hard pressed to match its performance of 1996, not least the steep rally from September to December which took the 10-year yield briefly to 7.0 percent, a near three-year low. More dramatic was the tightening in the spread to the U.S..

There was a fairly mixed response to the outlook for end-1997 but the consensus was for a yield backing up to 8.0 percent from the current level of around 7.50 percent as the domestic economy picks up and the United States is forced to tighten policy, causing U.S. yields to spike.

However, some houses believe there is scope for a further easing in monetary policy, that growth will be contained for most of 1997 and inflation will remain subdued, thus keeping yields relatively low.

It was Australia's much improved inflation outlook in 1996 that caused the Australian/U.S. 10-year yield differential to shrink to the mid-80 basis points level from around 250 basis points and one the key factors in the Reserve Bank cutting official interest rates three times in the second half of 1996.
Median forecasts for the spread centre on 140 basis points compared with a current 110 basis points.
Some economists still see scope for a further tightening in this yield differential as the local economy outperforms on the inflation front, although the bulk of the narrowing is over.

However, there is also a school of thought that the worries over the U.S. economy from a bond perspective have been overdone and the Fed will maintain a steady policy for sometime, while the local market will underperform as growth picks up, which will see spreads again widen sharply.

CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT - Despite the already-released 1.2 percent rise in imports in November, the CAD is expected to have held fairly steady in the month. After two months of a trade deficit, exports will need to rise by around 1.6 percent to see a return to the trade surplus of mid-year. Some economists said that while the current account stabilised and receded as a market concern in 1996, there was a real danger that it would begin to widen from the beginning of 1997 and would again become a prime concern of the markets.

RETAIL TRADE - Further correction from September's 3.7 percent fall is expected after October's 1.4 percent rise was seen as weak by the market. The rise, however, would do little to change the underlying picture of continuing soft consumer demand, and economists said it would be more interesting to see spending patterns over the Christmas and New Year sales period, especially to see if the December 11 rate cut had any impact.

BUILDING APPROVALS - Continuing the recent volatility in this series, most expect a fall in November approvals to follow the 12.8 percent rise seen in October. However, as that rise followed an 8.6 percent fall in September, a smaller drop is expected. Some were expecting a small rise, and said this would fit in with some signs of strength in approvals towards the end of 1996. The December 11 rate cut, and flow through mortgage rate reductions, was expected to have given the housing sector a boost going into 1997.
